analysis.one_liner: Imposes a fee on coal, oil, and natural gas and rebates most of the money to households.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Sanders with one Democratic cosponsor, was never taken up by the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died at the end of the 113th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge a fee starting at $20 per ton of carbon dioxide on coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers, rising about 5.6% each year. It returns three-fifths of the money as monthly rebates to every legal U.S. resident, sends some to weatherization, job training for fossil fuel workers, clean energy loans, and deficit reduction, and closes the loophole exempting fracking from the Safe Drinking Water Act while requiring disclosure of fracking chemicals. It never left committee and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households, especially lower-income ones: the monthly carbon rebate would give every legal resident the same payment, so households with smaller energy bills would come out ahead. Workers in the fossil fuel industry would get $1 billion a year for ten years in retraining and transition help, and low-income homes would get $5 billion a year for weatherization. Communities facing climate impacts would get adaptation funding.

how_it_helps.text: Charges $20 per ton of carbon dioxide on coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers, rising 5.6% a year for eleven years, making dirty energy more expensive relative to clean energy [S3].
Returns three-fifths of the fee revenue as a monthly rebate to every legal U.S. resident, with an EPA office created to help households sign up and administrative costs capped at 1 percent [S3].
Directs $7.5 billion a year for ten years to ease costs for energy-intensive industries, with at least a quarter reserved for their energy efficiency investments [S3].
Provides $5 billion a year for ten years for the Weatherization Assistance Program for Low-Income Persons, which insulates homes to cut heating and cooling bills [S3].
Provides $1 billion a year for ten years for job training and transition assistance for people employed by the fossil fuel industry [S3].
Funds the Sustainable Technologies Finance Program with $5 billion a year through 2022 for loans and loan guarantees to clean energy, efficiency, transit, and electric vehicle projects [S3].

Removes the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption for hydraulic fracturing, requires disclosure of fracking chemicals before and after use, and lets doctors get trade-secret chemical identities immediately in medical emergencies [S3] [S2].
Uses half of the import fee revenue to help communities adapt to climate change and harden critical infrastructure, including carpool facilities and electric vehicle charging [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies would pay the carbon fee on every ton they produce or import, and fossil fuel industries would face higher costs for energy-intensive goods. Some of the higher energy prices would reach consumers, though the monthly rebate is designed to leave most lower-income households financially ahead. Foreign manufacturers of steel, cement, glass, paper, and chemicals would pay an equivalent fee at the border unless their countries adopt their own carbon pricing.

drawbacks.text: Energy prices would rise, and the bill itself directs billions of dollars a year to cushion the economic impact on energy-intensive and trade-exposed industries, an acknowledgment that the fee raises costs for manufacturers, energy producers, and ultimately consumers [S3].

The bill allows only for confidentiality on chemical formulas in non-emergency disclosure, meaning some fracking chemical information the industry treats as trade secrets would still be shielded from public view [S3].

A carbon fee this high and rising would concentrate costs on regions and workers dependent on coal and fossil fuel jobs; the $1 billion annual transition fund is small relative to the employment base of the coal, oil, and gas sectors.
The border carbon fee would raise the price of imported steel, cement, aluminum, and other goods, which could raise costs for builders and manufacturers that use those materials [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is strongly weighted toward households: three-fifths of the revenue goes out in equal monthly rebates, so most lower-income families would pay less in fees than they receive back, and the bill funds weatherization and job training rather than just handing the money to industry. The main real cost is higher energy prices for everything, with transition support that may be too small for fossil-fuel-dependent communities. On the merits, the bill looks like a net gain for ordinary people and a real cost to fossil fuel producers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and no committee vote, hearing, or floor action ever followed before the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on February 14, 2013, with Senator Barbara Boxer as a co-sponsor [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no committee markup, no hearing recorded in the action history, no floor vote [S5].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers avoided a fee starting at $20 per ton that would have risen each year, and avoided new fracking disclosure requirements under the Safe Drinking Water Act. Households and communities waiting on the rebate, weatherization, and adaptation funding got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided the fee

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California, chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; no markup, hearing, or vote was scheduled in the two years before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded vote, so no party breakdown exists. The bill had one Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support, and it never advanced far enough for the full Senate to weigh in.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: Would have paid a fee starting at $20 per ton of carbon dioxide on every ton of coal, petroleum, and natural gas they produce or import, rising 5.6% annually for eleven years. The fee would raise their costs and push energy prices toward cleaner alternatives, a cost the industry would otherwise pass through to customers.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies conducting hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: Would have lost the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption for fracking and faced mandatory disclosure of chemicals used before and after fracking operations, plus new civil penalties for underground injection violations.

industries.industry: Importers of steel, cement, glass, aluminum, paper, and chemicals
industries.note: Would have paid a carbon equivalency fee at the border to match the cost domestic producers face, raising the price of imported industrial goods unless their home countries adopted equivalent carbon policies.

industries.industry: Clean energy and technology firms (solar, wind, batteries, transit, efficiency)
industries.note: Would have received $5 billion a year in loan guarantees and financing through the Sustainable Technologies Finance Program, plus additional research and deployment funding from the fee revenue.
Would have received $7.5 billion a year for ten years to offset economic impacts of the carbon fee, with at least a quarter reserved for energy efficiency investments in those industries.
